Telekomunikasi No.1, Bandung 40257, West Java, Indonesia 33220014@mahasiswa.itb.ac.id; huriantividya@telkomuniversity.ac.id _Abstract: This paper proposes a constraint-driven hierarchical user clustering framework to_ enhance the performance of Power-Domain Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (PD-NOMA) systems. Leveraging Ward's agglomerative hierarchical clustering with two practical constraints, namely a maximum of 8 users per cluster and an angular span limit of 60°, the proposed framework forms spatially compact, interference-aware clusters that ensure operationally feasible successive interference cancellation (SIC). Simulation results averaged over 30 independent random user distributions demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms unconstrained hierarchical clustering, K-Means clustering, and conventional NOMA. At 30 dBm with 30 users, the method achieves 281.45 Mbps, approximately 23% higher than unconstrained hierarchical clustering (229.03 Mbps), significantly above K-Means clustering (228.19 Mbps), and far exceeding conventional NOMA (54.97 Mbps). The near-identical performance of K-Means and unconstrained hierarchical clustering confirms that the performance bottleneck lies not in the choice of algorithm but in the absence of constraint-aware spatial grouping. Under constraint-driven clustering, the average sum rate scales from 246.79 Mbps at 20 users to 443.99 Mbps at 50 users, establishing the scalability of the framework for dense and non-terrestrial network deployments. _Keywords: Hierarchical Clustering; PD-NOMA; Sum Rate Optimization; Constraint-driven_ Clustering; K-Means **1\. Introduction** Power-Domain Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (PD-NOMA) has emerged as a promising multiple access technique for future wireless communication systems, particularly in the context of 5G and beyond [1][2]. Unlike traditional Orthogonal Multiple Access (OMA), which allocates orthogonal resources such as time, frequency, or code to different users, PD-NOMA enables multiple users to share the same time-frequency resource block by leveraging power-domain multiplexing [3]. This approach significantly enhances spectral efficiency and supports massive connectivity, making it suitable for ultra-dense networks and Internet of Things (IoT) applications [4][5]. However, as a key enabler for future sixth-generation (6G) networks, PD-NOMA faces practical deployment challenges due to the nature of successive interference cancellation (SIC) at the receiver, which requires careful management of intra-cluster interference to ensure reliable decoding performance [6][7]. Simultaneous transmission from multiple users over the same resource introduces severe intra-cell interference, especially when users with similar channel conditions are grouped together. This interference becomes more pronounced in high-density scenarios where the number of users exceeds the available degrees of freedom, leading to degraded system performance and reduced total data rate. To mitigate the detrimental effects of inter-user interference in PD-NOMA systems, various techniques have been proposed in the literature. One widely adopted method is user pairing based on channel gain differences, where users with significantly different channel strengths are paired to exploit successive interference cancellation (SIC) at the receiver side [8]. This concept has Received: April 10th, 2026. Accepted: June 26th, 2026 ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) also been extended to structured groupings beyond pairs: for instance, [9] demonstrated that partitioning users into small, two-user clusters based on channel gain disparity not only reduces SIC decoding complexity but also enhances overall system performance by maximizing sum rate. Their results further indicate that simply pairing users with the strongest and weakest channels does not always yield optimal sum rate, suggesting that a more nuanced selection criterion is necessary. Other approaches include beamforming optimization, power allocation algorithms, and advanced clustering strategies that group users based on their spatial distribution or channel characteristics [10][11][12]. Spatial user clustering has also been explored in [13] through static sectorization within a cell, which achieves significant improvements in sum rate compared to conventional NOMA. However, this approach suffers from limited effectiveness due to its reliance on manually predefined region divisions, lacking the adaptability and automation required for dynamic network environments. To address this limitation, automated clustering techniques have been proposed using machine learning, particularly unsupervised learning methods such as k-means clustering, which partitions users into groups based on distinct channel gains to reduce intracluster interference [14]. However, k-means clustering is fundamentally designed to minimize intra-cluster variance by grouping data points that are as similar and spatially close to each other as possible, a property that is inherently misaligned with the requirements of PD-NOMA systems. In PD-NOMA, effective successive interference cancellation (SIC) at the receiver depends critically on sufficient channel gain disparity among co-clustered users, meaning that users within the same cluster must exhibit significantly different received signal strengths so that the SIC decoder can sequentially and reliably separate each user's signal. Grouping users with similar channel gains, as k-means naturally tends to do, leads to ambiguous power levels at the decoder, increasing residual interference and ultimately degrading the achievable sum rate. Furthermore, k-means does not inherently account for the spatial correlation among users, thereby underutilizing the spatial diversity offered by directional antennas or sectorized coverage. This limitation has been confirmed empirically in recent studies on unsupervised clustering for NOMA systems, where agglomerative hierarchical clustering (AHC) consistently outperforms k-means in terms of system throughput and connectivity by determining the number of clusters adaptively without requiring this parameter as a prerequisite [15][16][17]. For these reasons, k-means clustering is not included as a performance baseline in this study, as its fundamental optimization objective is structurally misaligned with the core requirement of PD-NOMA where sufficient inter-user channel gain disparity within each cluster is a prerequisite for reliable SIC decoding rather than an undesirable artifact to be minimized. More recently, [18] introduced a user clustering scheme tailored for the coexistence of near-field (NF) and far-field (FF) communications, employing a coalitional game-based algorithm to jointly optimize beam assignment and SIC decoding order. While their simulation results demonstrate notable performance gains, the work still does not sufficiently address key practical challenges such as multi-user mobility and adaptive beamforming under dynamic channel conditions, factors that are essential for real-world deployment. Collectively, these studies highlight the need for a flexible, spatially aware, and constraint-aware clustering framework that can dynamically adapt to both user distribution and operational requirements in next-generation wireless networks, including non-terrestrial network scenarios such as HAPS and LEO satellite systems where automated geometry-aware grouping is essential [19][20]. In this paper, we propose a constraint-driven hierarchical user clustering framework for PD-NOMA systems to enhance total sum rate performance while effectively mitigating intra-cluster interference. The proposed method leverages spatial sectorization and hierarchical clustering to group users based on both their channel gains and geographical proximity. By dividing the cell into multiple sectors and applying a hierarchical clustering algorithm, users are organized into clusters that minimize interference within each group while maximizing overall system throughput. The clustering process is guided by constraints related to channel gain disparity and spatial separation, ensuring that users with similar propagation conditions are only grouped if ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) they are sufficiently separated in space. This dual consideration enables improved SIC performance and reduces the likelihood of decoding failure due to strong residual interference. The main contributions of this work are threefold: 1) We propose a constraint integrated hierarchical user clustering framework for PD NOMA systems in which practical system constraints, namely a maximum cluster size and an angular span limit, are embedded directly into Ward's agglomerative merging process rather than applied as post processing rules, thereby producing interference aware user groups that are both mathematically compact and operationally feasible for SIC. 2) We integrate these physical-layer constraints directly into the agglomerative clustering process, ensuring that the resulting clusters are not only mathematically compact but also operationally feasible for successive interference cancellation (SIC). 3) We demonstrate the scalability and adaptability of the proposed framework under varying user densities, establishing its suitability for real-world deployment in dense or non-terrestrial networks where automated, geometry-aware user grouping is essential. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system model, which discusses the proposed constraint-driven hierarchical user clustering methodology, including the clustering algorithm. Section III describes the simulation results and performance analysis, followed by conclusions and future research directions in Section IV. **2\. System Model** This section presents the system model for the proposed constraint-driven hierarchical user clustering framework in Power-Domain Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (PD-NOMA) systems. The considered scenario is a single-cell downlink network where a base station (BS) serves multiple users distributed within a circular cell area. The BS employs sectorized transmission, dividing the coverage region into multiple sectors to improve spatial reuse and reduce inter-sector interference. Users are grouped into clusters based on their channel conditions and spatial locations using an agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithm with Ward’s method, subject to practical constraints: a maximum of 8 users per cluster and a maximum angular coverage of 60° per cluster. The selection of 8 users per cluster is informed by prior work [21] which identifies 4–5 users per cluster as conducive to reliable SIC operation. With 30 users and an average of 6.4 clusters, the proposed configuration yields approximately 4.7 users per cluster, well within this range. The 60° angular span constraint is derived from practical beamforming considerations: a 60° sector corresponds to a standard 6-sector cell deployment, ensuring compatibility with conventional sectorized antenna systems. This value is also consistent with the expected cluster count: with 30 users and a target occupancy of 4–5 users per cluster, the algorithm naturally forms approximately 6–7 clusters, yielding a natural angular budget of 360°/6 = 60° per cluster, directly linking the upper bound to the system's user load and the 6-sector cell topology. This approach ensures that clusters remain compact both in terms of channel gain disparity and spatial distribution, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of successive interference cancellation (SIC) at the receiver side. Each cluster 𝐾𝐾𝑘𝑘 contains a subset of users grouped based on_ angular proximity, while strictly adhering to the imposed constraints. Within each cluster, users are scheduled using PD-NOMA, where power allocation follows a predefined rule (e.g., proportional to channel gain) to enable SIC at the receiver side. This system model enables scalable and interference-aware resource allocation, where the number of clusters 𝐾𝐾 is not fixed but dynamically determined by the clustering algorithm based on user distribution and constraint satisfaction. The resulting cluster structure serves as the basis for evaluating sum rate performance under various network loads and transmit power levels. To facilitate optimal user grouping in a SIC-based NOMA scenario, we propose a constrained hierarchical clustering approach. This method is designed to form clusters that are spatially compact and homogeneous in channel characteristics, while simultaneously adhering to practical system constraints—namely, a maximum number of users per cluster and a maximum angular coverage per cluster. The procedure not only minimizes intra-cluster variance but also ensures technical feasibility for stable and efficient SIC operation. The process begins with initialization: each user 𝑢𝑢𝑖𝑖 is treated as an individual cluster, resulting in 𝑁𝑁 singleton clusters at the outset. For each cluster, a centroid is computed as a joint representation of spatial location and channel gain. Mathematically, the centroid of cluster 𝐶𝐶𝑖𝑖 is defined as: 𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐(𝐶𝐶𝑖𝑖) = (𝑥𝑥𝑖𝑖 ,𝑦𝑦𝑖𝑖 , _ℎ𝑖𝑖) (1)_ where (𝑥𝑥𝑖𝑖,𝑦𝑦𝑖𝑖) denotes the two-dimensional coordinates of the user, and ℎ𝑖𝑖 represents its channel gain. This three-dimensional representation enables the clustering mechanism to account for both geometric proximity and signal strength, two critical factors for SIC performance. Following initialization, clusters are iteratively merged using Ward’s method. In each iteration, the pair of clusters 𝐶𝐶𝑎𝑎 and 𝐶𝐶𝑏𝑏 with the smallest Ward distance is selected for merging into a new cluster. The Ward distance between two clusters 𝐴𝐴 and 𝐵𝐵 is given by: 𝑑𝑑(𝐴𝐴,𝐵𝐵) = |𝐴𝐴||𝐵𝐵| |𝐴𝐴|+|𝐵𝐵| . ‖𝑥̅𝑥𝐴𝐴 − 𝑥̅𝑥𝐵𝐵‖2 (2) where:

  * ∣𝐴𝐴∣ and ∣𝐵𝐵∣ denote the number of users in clusters 𝐴𝐴 and 𝐵𝐵, respectively,
  * 𝑥̅𝑥𝐴𝐴 dan 𝑥̅𝑥𝐵𝐵 are the centroids of the respective clusters, computed as the arithmetic mean of the (𝑥𝑥, 𝑦𝑦, ℎ) vectors of all users within each cluster,
  * ∥⋅∥2 denotes the squared Euclidean distance between centroids. This metric mathematically minimizes the increase in within-cluster variance upon merging, thereby promoting the formation of dense and homogeneous clusters. Such homogeneity is crucial in NOMA systems, as it enables more reliable SIC decoding with minimal residual interference among users within the same cluster. After each merge, the centroid of the newly formed cluster is recomputed as the average of the spatial coordinates and channel gains of all its members. However, the merging process does not terminate merely when a target number of clusters is reached. Instead, two practical constraints are enforced iteratively to guarantee system feasibility[13]: 1. Cluster Size Constraint: If any cluster 𝐾𝐾𝑖𝑖 exceeds the maximum allowable number of users per cluster (e.g., 8 users), it is split into smaller sub-clusters. This partitioning can be performed based on pairwise distances or channel gain differences among users, preserving intra-subcluster homogeneity.


  2. Angular Span Constraint: If the angular span of a cluster (i.e., the angular separation between its outermost users, as seen from base station) exceeds a predefined threshold (e.g., 60°), the cluster is divided according to angular sectors. For instance, users may be reassigned into narrower angular intervals (e.g., 0°–30°, 30°–60°, etc.). This limits spatial dispersion, ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) enhances beamforming focus, and reduces inter-cluster interference, key considerations for maintaining high signal quality and SIC reliability. It is also worth noting that a practical lower bound on the angular span exists, governed by the half-power beamwidth (HPBW) of the antenna array employed at the base station [22]. Clusters whose angular span falls below this threshold cannot be spatially isolated by the beamformer and should therefore be merged or handled as a single beam group [23]. For a typical 8-element uniform linear array with half-wavelength element spacing, this lower bound is approximately 12–15° [24], implying that the effective operating range of the angular span constraint lies between this minimum beamwidth and the 60° upper bound adopted in this study. The iterative process of merging and constraint enforcement continues as long as at least two clusters remain and a feasible merge exists, that is, a candidate merge that does not immediately violate either constraint. The algorithm terminates when no further feasible merge is available, at which point the remaining clusters collectively form the final valid partition. The algorithm then outputs a final set of valid clusters 𝐾𝐾={𝐾𝐾1,𝐾𝐾2, …,𝐾𝐾k}, each satisfying both structural and geometric requirements. This set serves as the input for subsequent power allocation and user scheduling in the NOMA transmission phase. Figure 2. Flowchart of the proposed constraint-driven hierarchical user clustering algorithm for PD-NOMA ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) The overall workflow of the proposed algorithm is summarized in Figure 2. As illustrated, _the algorithm initializes M singleton clusters with centroids defined by Equation (1), then_ repeatedly selects the pair with minimum Ward distance given by Equation (2) for merging. After each merge, two sequential constraint checks are applied: (i) if cluster size exceeds 8 users, the cluster is split to restore intra-cluster homogeneity; (ii) if angular span exceeds 60°, the cluster is divided into narrower angular sectors to preserve beamforming focus and SIC reliability. Each constraint violation triggers a return to the Ward distance computation, ensuring all subsequent merges operate on constraint-compliant clusters. This iterative loop continues _until no further feasible merges remain, yielding K valid clusters that serve directly as input to_ the Sequential Power Allocation (SePA) and PD-NOMA transmission stages described in Equations (3) through (9). Simulation Results** In this section, we present a performance comparison between user clustering using standard hierarchical clustering and constraint-driven hierarchical clustering. A total of 30 users are randomly distributed across the cell area, with each simulation run repeated over 30 independent random user configurations to ensure statistical reliability and account for spatial variability. The system operates with a bandwidth 𝐵𝐵 = 5 MHz. For both clustering approaches, Ward’s linkage method is employed within an agglomerative (bottom-up) hierarchical framework, where each user is initially treated as a singleton cluster and progressively merged based on minimizing intra-cluster variance. In the case of constraint-driven hierarchical clustering, two practical constraints are enforced: a maximum of 8 users per cluster and a maximum angular span of 60° per cluster. These constraints are integrated into the merging process to ensure that resulting clusters remain feasible for NOMA transmission under realistic beamforming and SIC decoding conditions. Figure 3. User Distribution (a) Unconstrained Hierarchical Clustering and (b) Constraint-driven Hierarchical Clustering Figure 3 presents a comparative visualization of user clustering outcomes under two hierarchical clustering (HC) strategies in a PD-NOMA system with 30 randomly distributed users. In the unconstrained approach (Figure 3a), clustering is performed solely based on angular similarity using Ward’s linkage on a unit-circle embedding of user angles, without imposing any limits on cluster size or angular span. This results in only four large clusters that aggregate users across wide angular ranges, often combining distant or sparsely distributed users into a single group. While this method minimizes intra-cluster variance in the abstract feature space, it ignores practical limitations of multi-user NOMA decoding. In contrast, the constraint-driven HC (Figure 3b) enforces two key rules: each cluster must contain no more than eight users and its angular span must not exceed 60 degrees. These constraints reflect realistic operational boundaries for effective successive interference cancellation (SIC) in PD-NOMA. Consequently, the algorithm forms seven smaller, spatially compact clusters that better isolate groups of users with similar channel conditions, thereby creating favorable conditions for power-domain multiplexing and interference management. Despite increasing the number of clusters and thus reducing the transmit power allocated per cluster, the constraint-driven approach achieves a significantly higher total sum rate (327.9 Mbps) compared to the unconstrained variant (192.7 Mbps). This performance gain arises because PD-NOMA efficiency deteriorates sharply when too many users share the same resource block. In large clusters, weak users receive insufficient power and suffer from overwhelming interference from stronger co-cluster users, leading to decoding failure and rate collapse. By limiting cluster size and angular dispersion, the constrained method ensures that intra-cluster channel disparities remain manageable, enabling reliable SIC and more balanced rate allocation. The result is a net improvement in spectral efficiency, demonstrating that structural constraints rather than being restrictive can act as enablers of higher system throughput in NOMA-based networks. These findings underscore a critical insight for NOMA system design: optimal clustering is not merely about minimizing geometric or angular distance, but about shaping clusters to match the operational limits of the underlying multiple access scheme. The proposed constraint-driven HC framework provides a lightweight yet effective mechanism to align user grouping with PD-NOMA’s decoding requirements, without requiring complex optimization or channel state ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) feedback beyond basic angular information. This approach is particularly valuable in scenarios such as HAPS or dense cellular deployments, where user distributions are irregular and dynamic. By prioritizing cluster quality over quantity, the method achieves robust sum rate gains across diverse spatial configurations, establishing constraint-aware hierarchical clustering as a practical and scalable strategy for next-generation non-orthogonal multiple access systems. (a) Unconstrained HC (4 clusters) (b) Constraint-driven HC (7 clusters) Figure 4. Dendrograms illustrating cluster formation under (a) unconstrained and (b) constraint-driven HC for 30 users The dendrograms presented in Figure 4 provide a structural insight into how the two hierarchical clustering strategies partition the user set based on angular similarity. This figure corresponds directly to the clustering outcomes visualized in Figure 3, for a PD-NOMA system with 30 randomly distributed users. In Figure 4(a), the unconstrained HC method employs Ward’s linkage to merge users in a way that minimizes intra-cluster variance, ultimately forming only four clusters when the dendrogram is cut at a distance threshold of d = 1.5. This indicates that the algorithm prioritizes global compactness over local granularity, grouping users who are relatively close in angular space even if they span wide sectors or contain many users. The resulting large clusters reflect a natural outcome of agglomerative clustering without operational boundaries, which may be suitable for systems where resource allocation is not limited by physical beamforming or decoding complexity. However, this approach does not account for practical NOMA constraints such as maximum user count per group or angular spread, which can lead to inefficient power allocation and degraded performance in multi-user scenarios. In contrast, Figure 4(b) depicts the dendrogram for constraint-driven HC, where the clustering process is guided by explicit rules: no cluster may exceed eight users, and its angular span must remain within 60 degrees. To satisfy these conditions, the algorithm selects a lower cut distance (d = 0.95), resulting in seven distinct clusters. This earlier termination of merging reflects a deliberate trade-off: instead of allowing large, heterogeneous groups, the method favors smaller, more homogeneous clusters that better align with the decoding requirements of PD-NOMA. The dendrogram structure reveals tighter subgroups near the bottom, indicating users with very similar angles being grouped first, while higher merges are suppressed to prevent violating the imposed limits. This structural adjustment ensures that each cluster remains manageable for successive interference cancellation, thereby enhancing overall system reliability and spectral efficiency despite the increased number of clusters. These dendrogram comparisons highlight a fundamental principle in constrained optimization for NOMA systems: imposing practical limitations during clustering does not merely restrict flexibility but actively improves performance by shaping the problem space to match the capabilities of the underlying access scheme. While the unconstrained method produces fewer, larger clusters that appear mathematically optimal in terms of variance reduction, it fails to consider the real-world implications of multi-user interference and power allocation inefficiency. On the other hand, the constraint-driven approach leverages domain knowledge, such as user density and angular dispersion, to create clusters that are operationally ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) viable and conducive to high-rate transmission. The visual difference in cut levels and cluster counts between the two dendrograms serves as a clear indicator of how constraints reshape the clustering hierarchy, transforming what might seem like a restriction into a strategic enabler of higher sum rate and more robust communication performance in PD-NOMA networks. Figure 5. Average sum rate versus transmit power for constraint-driven HC, unconstrained HC, K-Means clustering, and conventional NOMA in a 30-user PD-NOMA system Figure 5 presents the average sum rate performance of four transmission strategies: constraint-driven HC, unconstrained HC, K-Means clustering, and conventional NOMA, as a function of transmit power ranging from 20 to 50 dBm. The results are averaged over 30 independent random user distributions, each consisting of 30 users uniformly scattered within a 50 m radius around the base station. This averaging ensures statistical reliability and mitigates the impact of channel randomness due to shadowing and Rayleigh fading. As expected, all four curves exhibit a monotonically increasing trend with rising transmit power, reflecting the fundamental relationship between signal strength and achievable data rate. However, the performance gap between the strategies remains consistent across the power range, indicating that the relative advantage of constraint-driven clustering is robust under varying power conditions. At the reference point of 30 dBm, which corresponds to 1 Watt of transmit power, the performance differences become particularly evident. Constraint-driven HC achieves an average sum rate of approximately 281.45 Mbps, while unconstrained HC yields 229.03 Mbps, K-Means clustering produces 228.19 Mbps, and conventional NOMA lags significantly at just 54.97 Mbps. A particularly noteworthy observation is the near-identical performance of K-Means clustering and unconstrained HC across the entire power range, with a difference of less than 1 Mbps at 30 dBm. This result is not coincidental. K-Means clustering groups users based on minimum Euclidean distance to spatial centroids, which tends to place geographically proximate users and consequently users with similar channel gains into the same cluster. As discussed in Section I, this grouping strategy is fundamentally misaligned with the requirements of PD-NOMA, where sufficient channel gain disparity among co-clustered users is a prerequisite for reliable SIC decoding. The convergence of K-Means and unconstrained HC performance thus confirms that the absence of operational constraints, regardless of the underlying clustering algorithm employed, systematically leads to suboptimal cluster formation that degrades SIC efficiency and limits achievable sum rate. This finding provides empirical validation for the ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) argument presented in Section I that K-Means is not a suitable baseline for PD-NOMA user grouping, and that the performance bottleneck lies not in the choice of clustering algorithm but in the absence of constraint-aware spatial grouping. In contrast, constraint-driven HC achieves a gain of approximately 52.42 Mbps over unconstrained HC and 226.48 Mbps over conventional NOMA at 30 dBm, reinforcing the central thesis of this work: structural constraints are not merely operational restrictions but strategic enablers of higher system throughput in PD-NOMA networks. By enforcing a maximum of 8 users per cluster and an angular span limit of 60°, the proposed framework ensures that each cluster contains users with sufficiently diverse channel conditions and compact spatial distributions, enabling reliable SIC decoding and more balanced power allocation across users. The consistent performance superiority of constraint-driven HC across the entire power range demonstrates that intelligently shaping user groups according to these operational limits leads to better interference management, more effective resource utilization, and robust decoding reliability, qualities that neither unconstrained HC, K-Means clustering, nor conventional NOMA can achieve without the integration of constraint-driven spatial grouping. Figure 6. Number of clusters formed per run (30 users, 30 dBm, 30 independent random user distributions) Figure 6 illustrates the number of clusters dynamically formed by constraint-driven HC and unconstrained HC across 30 independent random user distributions. Constraint-driven HC produces an average of 6.43 clusters per run, which, since cluster counts are necessarily integer values, corresponds to a practical operating point of 6 to 7 clusters in the vast majority of runs (k=6 in 15 of 30 runs, k=7 in 11 of 30 runs). This average of 6.43 clusters, rounded to 7 yields an average occupancy of approximately 4.7 users per cluster for a 30-user system, which falls within the range identified in prior literature as conducive to reliable SIC operation [21]. In contrast, unconstrained HC forms an average of only 5.0 clusters, occasionally collapsing to as few as 4 clusters in 6 of the 30 runs, resulting in groups with up to 7–8 users that exceed practical SIC decoding limits. The shaded region between the two curves highlights the consistent gap in cluster granularity introduced by the constraint enforcement mechanism. This gap reflects the direct effect of the angular span constraint: whenever a candidate merge would produce a cluster exceeding 60° of angular coverage or more than 8 users, the algorithm refrains from merging and retains the current partition, resulting in more clusters than unconstrained HC would naturally produce. Crucially, the number of clusters under constraint-driven HC remains bounded between 5 and 8 across all evaluated distributions, demonstrating that the framework adapts dynamically to each user topology without producing excessively fragmented or over-consolidated cluster structures. ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) It is worth noting that the algorithm does not actively minimize cluster occupancy. Although smaller cluster sizes such as 2–3 users per cluster would provide more favorable SIC decoding conditions due to greater channel gain disparity, achieving such occupancy with 30 users would require 10–15 clusters, significantly increasing system complexity. The adopted configuration of 8 users / 60° yields approximately 4.7 users per cluster and 6–7 clusters on average, representing a balance between sum rate performance and deployment practicality. Figure 7. Sum rate versus average Intra-Cluster Variance (30 users, 30 dBm, 30 independent random user distributions) Figure 7 presents the relationship between average intra-cluster variance (ICV) and sum rate for each of the 30 independent user distributions at 30 dBm, evaluated across constraint-driven HC, unconstrained HC, and K-Means clustering. The intra-cluster variance (ICV) used in this analysis is computed in the angular domain: each user is projected onto a unit circle using their angular position as observed from the base station, represented as the coordinate pair (cos 𝜃𝜃𝑖𝑖 , sin 𝜃𝜃𝑖𝑖), and ICV is defined as the average variance of these projected positions across all clusters in a given run. This metric quantifies the degree of angular compactness of the resulting clusters from the perspective of the BS, a low ICV indicates that users within each cluster occupy a narrow angular sector, which is favorable for coherent beamforming and effective SIC decoding in PD-NOMA systems, while a high ICV reflects wide angular dispersion that degrades interference management and reduces achievable sum rate. As observed in Figure 7, constraint-driven HC consistently occupies the low-ICV region across all 30 runs, with an average ICV of 0.0396 and an average sum rate of 281.45 Mbps. The downward-sloping trend line confirms that lower angular variance is reliably associated with higher sum rate, a direct result of the 60° angular span constraint, which explicitly limits the spread of users within each cluster as seen from the BS. Unconstrained HC exhibits a similar descending trend but with higher average ICV (0.0719) and lower average sum rate (229.03 Mbps), reflecting the absence of angular compactness enforcement during cluster formation. K-Means clustering, which groups users based on Euclidean proximity in coordinate space (x, y) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) rather than angular proximity from the BS, produces substantially higher average ICV (0.1342) and yields an average sum rate of 228.19 Mbps. The K-Means data points are widely scattered without a consistent directional trend, confirming that Euclidean proximity does not reliably translate into angular compactness from the BS perspective, and consequently does not produce the channel condition structure required for effective SIC in PD-NOMA. These results collectively demonstrate that the performance advantage of constraint-driven HC is structurally rooted in its explicit enforcement of angular compactness, which directly reduces intra-cluster interference and enables more reliable successive decoding across diverse user distribution patterns. Figure 8. Sum rate versus number of users for unconstrained HC and constraint-driven HC in a PD-NOMA system Figure 8 presents the average sum rate performance of unconstrained HC and constraint-driven HC across four different system loads: 20, 30, 40, and 50 users. All results are obtained at a fixed transmit power of 30 dBm and averaged over 30 independent random user distributions for each user count, consistent with the methodology applied in the transmit power analysis of Figure 5. This averaging ensures statistical robustness and accounts for channel variations due to shadowing and Rayleigh fading. As shown in the figure, both strategies exhibit increasing sum rate with higher user density, which is expected since more users contribute to the total system throughput. However, the performance gap between the two methods widens as the number of users increases, indicating that constraint-driven clustering becomes increasingly advantageous in larger systems. At every user count, constraint-driven HC consistently outperforms unconstrained HC. At 20 users, constraint-driven HC achieves 246.79 Mbps compared to 217.64 Mbps for unconstrained HC, representing a gain of approximately 29.15 Mbps. At the reference configuration of 30 users, constraint-driven HC achieves 281.45 Mbps compared to 229.03 Mbps for unconstrained HC, representing a gain of approximately 52.42 Mbps, consistent with the performance observed at 30 dBm in Figure 5, confirming the internal consistency of the simulation framework. The advantage grows progressively with system size: at 40 users, the difference reaches 83.86 Mbps (348.16 Mbps vs. 264.30 Mbps), and at 50 users, the gap widens to approximately 158.45 Mbps (443.99 Mbps vs. 285.54 Mbps). This trend confirms that constraint-driven HC scales better under high user density. The reason lies in its ability to maintain cluster quality: by enforcing limits on cluster size and angular span, it prevents the formation of overly large or heterogeneous groups that degrade NOMA efficiency. In contrast, unconstrained HC tends to merge distant users into single clusters, leading to poor interference management and inefficient power allocation among weak users. ![image](data:image/jpeg;base64,) However, it is important to note that while increasing the number of users leads to higher sum rate, it also results in a larger number of clusters, particularly under constraint-driven HC, which enforces strict limits on cluster size and angular span. At 50 users, the algorithm typically generates 10 or more clusters, each requiring a dedicated beam and independent power allocation. This raises practical concerns regarding system complexity, including increased computational load for beamforming, higher hardware demands on the transmitter, and greater signaling overhead for cluster assignment and SIC ordering. Therefore, although constraint-driven HC delivers superior spectral efficiency, its deployment in large-scale networks must be carefully balanced against implementation constraints. Future work should explore adaptive clustering strategies that dynamically adjust cluster granularity based on available hardware resources and real-time traffic conditions, ensuring optimal trade-offs between throughput and system complexity. **4\. Conclusions** This paper has proposed and validated a constraint-driven hierarchical user clustering framework for PD-NOMA systems. Three key contributions are confirmed through simulation. First, the joint incorporation of a maximum angular span of 60° and a maximum of 8 users per cluster into Ward's agglomerative clustering reliably produces spatially compact, interferenceaware user groups across all 30 evaluated random distributions, directly addressing the SIC feasibility requirement of PD-NOMA. Second, at 30 dBm with 30 users, the proposed method achieves 281.45 Mbps, outperforming unconstrained hierarchical clustering by 52.42 Mbps and K-Means clustering by 53.26 Mbps, with both comparators converging to near-identical performance — confirming that the performance bottleneck lies not in the choice of clustering algorithm but in the absence of constraint-aware spatial grouping. The cluster structure analysis further shows that constraint-driven HC consistently produces the lowest average intra-cluster variance (0.0396), compared to 0.0719 for unconstrained HC and 0.1342 for K-Means, establishing a direct structural link between angular compactness and achievable sum rate. Third, the framework scales effectively with user density, with the sum rate increasing from 246.79 Mbps at 20 users to 443.99 Mbps at 50 users, and the performance gap over unconstrained HC widening from 29.15 Mbps to 158.45 Mbps, confirming that the proposed approach becomes increasingly advantageous as network density grows. For future research, this framework can be extended in several promising directions. First, mobility-aware clustering algorithms can be integrated to handle dynamic user movement while preserving cluster integrity under constraint boundaries. Second, machine learning techniques, particularly reinforcement learning or graph neural networks, can be employed to dynamically optimize cluster assignment and power allocation in real time, adapting to changing channel conditions and traffic demands. Third, the framework can be generalized to multi-cell scenarios, where inter-cell interference must be jointly managed with intra-cluster optimization. A particularly promising direction is the tighter integration of the clustering algorithm with the physical beamformer, for example by constraining cluster angular boundaries to align with quantized codebook directions or by incorporating the antenna array's half-power beamwidth as a hard lower bound on cluster angular span. Such integration would bring the proposed framework closer to deployment-ready beamforming systems. Finally, applying this constraint-driven clustering paradigm to emerging technologies such as non-terrestrial networks, mmWave and THz communications, or integrated sensing and communication systems [25] could unlock new opportunities for scalable, high-efficiency multi-user access in next-generation wireless networks. **5\.
